# CI Adoption Notes

This page covers adoption of generated CI and release automation on GitHub and
Codeberg.

## Generator Contract

Generated workflow files are owned by simit and include:

```text
# Generated by simit. Manual edits will be reported as ci=drift.
```

After the first non-check `simit init ci` run, simit persists effective CI options
in the existing `simit.toml` or Cargo metadata source. Projects without a config
get `simit.toml`. Flake-provided config must declare its strategy explicitly when
enabling release-plz; Simit does not create a second config source. The drift check is:

```sh
simit init ci --platform <forgejo|github> --check --diff
```

When a project has not yet persisted its CI options, the drift error still
prints the full regeneration command with the effective runtime, runner,
workspace, and optional gates so the migration path stays explicit.

Persisted CI settings look like:

```toml
[ci]
platform = "forgejo"
runtime = "nix"
runner = "atlas"
workspace = true
with_deny = true
with_audit = true
with_docs = true
with_msrv = true
```

## Release-plz on GitHub Actions

Newly enabling Rust publication on supported GitHub Actions projects selects
`release-plz`. Existing publishing setups retain their implicit or explicit
`members` / `coordinated` policy until explicitly migrated:

```sh
simit init ci --platform github --publish-crates --publish-strategy release-plz
# For a Cargo workspace, also pass --workspace.
simit init ci --check --diff
```

`--publish-strategy members|coordinated|release-plz` selects a strategy explicitly.
The older `--coordinated-publish[=false]` flag still maps to coordinated/members;
conflicting selections are rejected. An explicit `members` selection
is persisted even though it is the legacy default.
Release-plz requires crate publication to be enabled (`--publish-crates` or the
matching project setting), even when binary artifacts are requested. Artifact-only
generation keeps the legacy strategy rather than implicitly adopting release-plz.

Release-plz computes versions and per-package changelogs and orchestrates crates.io
publication and signed tags. Simit delivers its prepared release PR data and
verified crate archives from separate credentialed workers. Simit also owns configured binary builds, checksums, attestations and
hosted assets. In that arrangement `release-plz.toml` sets
`git_release_enable = false`, so only Simit creates the hosted release. For
crate-only projects release-plz also creates the hosted release. Single-crate tags
respect `[release].tag_prefix`; multi-crate tags are `<package>/v<version>`.
Use the release PR to release these projects instead of running `simit release`
or manually bumping/tagging versions.

The generated files are `release-plz.toml`, `.simit/release-plz.py`, and
`.github/workflows/release-plz.yaml`. `init ci --check` and registry auditing cover
all three. Generator-owned member/coordinated publishers are retired during
migration. Hand-written competing publishers or release-plz configuration must
be reconciled explicitly before generation; Simit reports their paths.
Migration follows literal local scripts and reusable workflows, respecting
workflow/job/step working directories and custom shell templates. Missing,
external or opaque local files, local actions and remote reusable workflows
require explicit reconciliation. `cargo publish`, `cargo release`, `cargo-release`
and `release-plz` invocations count as competing publishers.
Tracked and unignored local scripts are inspected regardless of extension;
ignored untracked build outputs are not source inputs. A generated-file marker
alone cannot exempt a publisher that the migration plan leaves active.
Environment assignments and supported wrapper options are consumed before
inspecting the executable. Opaque options such as directory changes or split-string
execution require explicit reconciliation instead of silently skipping a wrapper.
Variable-expanded executable names and shell `eval` also require reconciliation;
use literal executable names so a retained publisher cannot hide behind them.
The `actions-rs/cargo` command input is inspected; unresolved command expressions
require reconciliation. In explicit Python, Node, Ruby and PowerShell steps,
known native process-launch calls also expose literal local executables for
inspection, including multi-line argv lists. Arguments passed as data are not
treated as executables.
Native execution overrides such as Python's `executable=`, Python/Node `cwd` and
Ruby `chdir` require explicit reconciliation. Direct `env` shebangs consume
supported options and assignments before selecting the interpreter; computed or
unsupported forms fail closed.
Bash syntax trees also expose nested command/backtick and process substitutions,
including substitutions inside assignment values, parameter expansions and data
arguments. Their literal commands are inspected without evaluating them; malformed
substitutions require reconciliation. Single-quoted literal text is not executed.
This bounded scan is not a general program analyzer: review generated executables,
computed/downloaded commands and remote reusable workflows before enabling
publication.

Initial support includes Cargo and Nix runtimes, a single publishable crate
with binary releases, and ordinary multi-crate Cargo workspaces. Package
selectors, alternate registries, mixed-language monorepos, other CI providers,
and multi-publishable-crate workspaces with repository-wide binary releases are
rejected for an explicit release-plz selection. Unsupported new setups retain
the existing publishing default.

### Automation credentials and signing

Configure these repository secrets before enabling default-branch execution:

| Name                          | Purpose                                                                                |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN`           | Repository-scoped PAT with contents and pull-requests write access                     |
| `CRATES_IO_API_TOKEN`         | crates.io publication token                                                            |
| `RELEASE_PLZ_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` | Armored OpenPGP private key authorized by the committed `[release.signing].trust_root` |
| `RELEASE_PLZ_GPG_PASSPHRASE`  | Optional signing-key passphrase                                                        |

Set the repository variable `SIMIT_PUBLISHER_REVISION` to an independently
qualified immutable Simit revision with release-plz archive admission support.
An engine enrolled for the older tag publishers must be qualified and updated
before adopting this integration.

A repository-installed GitHub App is preferred over a PAT. To use one, set a
repository App ID variable and private-key secret, then configure:

```toml
[ci]
publish_crates = true
publish_strategy = "release-plz"

[ci.release_plz]
app_id_variable = "RELEASE_PLZ_APP_ID"
app_private_key_secret = "RELEASE_PLZ_APP_PRIVATE_KEY"
# Optional secret-name overrides:
registry_token_secret = "CRATES_IO_API_TOKEN"
signing_key_secret = "RELEASE_PLZ_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY"
signing_passphrase_secret = "RELEASE_PLZ_GPG_PASSPHRASE"
```

Workflow generation and `release secrets contract --json` share the same App-pair
and credential-name validation; an incomplete pair never falls back to a PAT contract.

Place these tables under `package.metadata.simit` or `workspace.metadata.simit`
when Cargo metadata is the existing config source. `token_secret` overrides the
PAT secret name when no App is configured. The generated App token is restricted
to this repository and contents/pull-requests write permission. The default
`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot trigger release-PR CI or the downstream tag workflows;
it is used only for read-only selection and update preparation. Git authentication
is repository-scoped and inherited by release-plz's temporary repositories. See the
[upstream token contract](https://release-plz.dev/docs/github/token).

`simit release secrets contract --platform github` includes the release-plz
secret/variable requirements. `simit release verify` uses that contract for required
credentials, including custom registry secrets and crate-only releases; it does
not also request an unused default registry secret. The workflow checks credentials before writes,
derives its Git identity from the authorized signing key's UID, enables
`tag.gpgSign`, probes signing, and deletes the private key material afterward.
Existing downstream signed-tag/trust-root admission remains required. This
integration uses an explicit crates.io token; it does not assume a pre-existing
trusted-publishing registration applies to the new workflow.

### Revision qualification and recovery

The CLI is pinned to release-plz **0.3.172** (reviewed source
`8b523fa6c4eb4992f18365ac50a196b4dc6a1013`). The fixed Linux worker verifies the
upstream GNU binary's SHA-256 before execution, independently of the project's
MSRV. Credential-free Nix jobs execute update preparation through `nix develop -c`;
credentialed jobs use the verified standalone binary and data-only operations.
Workflow actions use the shared immutable action registry.
The generated config uses `release_always = false`: ordinary default-branch
pushes update a release PR; merging that PR starts publication.

Release-plz may publish the last commit of a merged release PR rather than the
merge event's branch tip. Simit requires a same-repository generated release
branch and matching head/body receipt, verifies the original head's OpenPGP
signature against the event's committed trust root, and resolves that immutable
revision. Squashed PR heads are fetched with the read-only token when absent
from the event checkout. Simit runs project
checks and required gates on it in a credential-free job, and verifies packaged
archives with modern Cargo's unpublished-workspace dependency staging. Merge commits select the PR head; squash merges select the squash
commit. Selection inspects the complete native push range, so later commits in
the same push cannot hide a release merge or replace its selected revision.
Only exact PR merge commits introduced by that push count. Multiple release PRs
in one push and incomplete/non-fast-forward history require reconciliation before
publication or PR preparation can advance. Publication rechecks selection, and a Cargo wrapper refuses any upload
from a different revision. Qualification of branch HEAD alone is insufficient.

The publication worker independently reconstructs every archive from the selected
Git tree with the qualified engine's data-only Cargo path. Project Cargo config,
wrappers, hooks, Nix expressions and build scripts never run with release
credentials. The release-plz Cargo adapter routes uploads through that same
archive verifier and registry transport, and refuses build-capable commands.
Before release-plz can upload or push any tag, Simit reconciles every existing
workspace version, including crates release-plz will skip. Each upload repeats
that check. A published archive must match its registry checksum and the qualified
package contents. Unchanged members may carry an older ancestral Git SHA; only
that provenance field may differ. Changed contents, dirty/non-ancestral source
bindings, wrong identities and yanked versions stop the entire release.

Release PR preparation runs `release-plz update` without release credentials,
including its available semver checks. A fresh worker admits only regular-file
changes to `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` and `CHANGELOG.md` into the Git index, then
signs and delivers that tree. It preserves an existing PR using an exact-head
lease and refuses to overwrite manual edits. Close or explicitly reconcile an
existing upstream-created release PR before the first generated update. A pushed
signed commit also binds the prepared summary and the exact prior PR body. Failed
PR creation/update API calls can resume without repushing; an already-delivered
response is a no-op. Recovery verifies the committed trust root, exact event
parent and admitted tree and never discards unrecognized/manual changes.
Superseded events never create or update a PR, including on retry. A current-source
successor may replace an interrupted older signed update only when its exact
prior-body binding still matches and its single source parent is ancestral to the
current event; it delivers newly admitted current-source data, not the stale tree.
Failed release qualification or publication also blocks the next PR update.

Each immutable push keeps a separate run with no in-progress cancellation. Its
selection job uses GitHub's native `queue: max` admission group: waiting behind
another selection job does not consume its 360-minute execution timeout. After
admission, Simit waits up to 350 minutes for the preceding default-branch run
through the read-only Actions API. A predecessor must have already completed its
own selection, so the budget excludes that predecessor's admission wait.
[GitHub queues up to 100 pending jobs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency#example-queueing-multiple-pending-runs);
overflow is canceled, and FIFO follows queue arrival, not event/run-number order.
Out-of-order admission fails rather than deadlocking the occupied slot. Failed,
canceled or timed-out predecessors block all later publication and PR preparation;
retry/reconcile them in run-number order before retrying blocked runs. Incomplete
provider history also fails closed. Actionlint 1.7.12 does not yet support `queue`;
Simit's Nix development/test environments use `nix/actionlint-queue.patch` to
validate `single|max` and reject `max` with literal `cancel-in-progress: true`,
without suppressing any other lint checks. Downstream lint environments need
equivalent queue support until upstream adds it.
Release PR delivery skips superseded default-branch revisions. Publication is
never canceled halfway through. Release-plz uploads
crates **before** pushing tags and skips versions already published on a retry.
A failed tag push can therefore leave a published crate without a tag; rerunning
does not promise tag repair. Inspect the failed run, the selected SHA, and crates.io
package contents before recovering. Have an authorized maintainer create and
verify the missing signed tag at that exact SHA, then push it with credentials
that trigger the binary workflows. Never move an existing published release tag
or republish different contents under the same version.

Simit's own Cargo metadata explicitly adopts this strategy. Live qualification
requires the automation token/App and authorized signing key to be provisioned.
Before downstream rollout, retain evidence of release-PR CI, the intended
revision's crates.io publication, a verified signed tag, and its binary release.

## Generic CI vs Release Publishing

### Execution ownership and duplicate work

Member CI runs repository formatting, full-flake validation, dependency audit,
dependency policy and declared integration gates once, in the first selected
member's workflow. Each member retains its own tests, Clippy, documentation,
MSRV and package checks. A project-wide `check_command` or Omnix replacement
has one CI owner; per-package release workflows keep their independent
publication prerequisites. Update required contexts when migrating existing
member workflows; the shared gate must remain required.

Rust/Nix CI honors `components = ["flake-evaluation"]` with
`nix flake check --no-build`. Selecting `"checks"` instead performs full flake
validation; selecting both does not repeat evaluation before that same full
check. The independent lane's all-system evaluation and Python's evaluation
plus selected check builds cover different scopes and remain separate.
An evaluation-only migration needs complete replacement build coverage before
it qualifies; a list of successful selected builds alone does not prove it.

Nextest replaces the ordinary test harness and retains separate Cargo doctests
for doctest-enabled library targets, including each feature mode. Binary-only
packages and `unit_tests_only` do not get invalid or out-of-scope doctest commands.
`unit_tests_only` selects library tests, or binary unit tests when the selected
packages have no library target; aggregate CI considers every selected member.
Omnix replacement suppresses generic Cargo tests and Clippy across Actions,
split-runner and Crow layouts. Omnix augmentation retains both by design.

To qualify PRs and validate default-branch pushes once per source, explicitly
set the repository's real default branch in the relevant policies:

```toml
[ci]
push_branches = ["trunk"]

[ci.nix_build]
push_branches = ["trunk"]
```

These are trigger filters, not successful job-level skips. Empty lists preserve
all branch pushes. The primary filter supports GitHub Actions Rust/Python/flake
and monorepo qualification CI;
the matrix filter supports GitHub Actions matrices, including grouped builds.
Projects requiring independent push/PR originals retain their existing
`separate_events` policies until their custody enrollment and required contexts
have migrated together. Combining branch filters with explicit `separate_events`
is rejected before generation. Release/tag triggers retain their separate policy.
`[prebuild].push_branches` filters the native prebuild's branch pushes the same
way; pull requests still run it and releases still reuse it via `workflow_call`.
Distinct MSRV, feature, platform, extracted-package, all-system evaluation and
fresh-execution checks are separate acceptance cases, not duplicate work.

### Simit's own CI ownership

Simit uses evaluation-only primary CI with these required execution owners:

| Coverage                                                                                                                          | Owner                       |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Formatting, flake evaluation, all-feature and no-default-feature tests/Clippy, Rustdoc, generator drift, package inventory        | `test`                      |
| Production package build and its filtered-source all-feature tests; dependency closure                                            | `qualify`                   |
| Locked advisory audit, dependency policy, filtered custody assets, public-package cache policy                                    | `qualify`                   |
| Complete production-generator regeneration and retained source/tree/binary/workflow evidence, including signed-release publishing | `qualify`                   |
| All workflow lint, including both signed-release publishers                                                                       | `qualify-release-generator` |

The full-flake check outputs remain available locally. CI avoids rebuilding
their formatting, Clippy, test and Rustdoc equivalents before native validation.
The source-filtered production package still builds and runs its tests separately.
Rustdoc's shell carries Rust dependency inputs and mdBook; site builds own Plinth.
Both push and PR originals remain explicitly enrolled for custody. Native-platform,
transport, observer-isolation and publisher-boundary qualifications retain their
independent workflows and required contexts.
Both replacement qualifiers cover every primary CI push branch, including branches
without an open pull request.
Their concurrency groups separate push and PR events, while newer revisions still
supersede older runs within each event stream.

### Native grouped Nix executor

Grouped workflows invoke `simit ci nix-group`. Before adopting regenerated
workflows, enroll the repository variable `SIMIT_CI_ENGINE_REVISION` with the
exact 40-character lowercase Git revision of a qualified Simit engine containing
that command. Provisioning builds `github:caniko/simit/<revision>#default`, not
the producer checkout, and retains the selected source revision and executable
SHA-256 in the evidence root. Missing or malformed enrollment and an engine
without the command fail the job. There is no moving-ref or Python fallback.
This read-only producer bootstrap is not enrollment for privileged completion
custody or release publishing; those engines have separate authority contracts.
Producer `extra_env` bindings apply only to setup, validation, execution and
diagnostic steps after provisioning. Engine provisioning clears shell startup
files and uses controlled Nix configuration and public substitution. Bootstrap
explicitly clears Nix `access-tokens` for its build, including tokens
installed by a preceding Nix action, and hashes the engine with `nix hash file`.
The immutable engine supports `x86_64-linux`, `aarch64-linux` and
`aarch64-darwin`. Known Intel macOS grouped runner labels reject during
generation; custom runners must pass the system guard before provisioning.
Grouped configuration cannot override reserved `SIMIT_CI_*`, `SIMIT_NIX_*` or
`INSTALLABLES` runtime inputs.
The pinned engine's closure is reused across runs through the GitHub Actions
cache key `simit-engine-v1-<revision>-<os>-<arch>`, so group jobs evaluate the
pin instead of compiling Simit each time. Provisioning, the source revision and
the executable digest evidence are unchanged; a miss or unreadable entry builds
normally. Like `cache_installables`, entries carry the trust of the
repository's default-branch runs.

The command reads the generated environment lists, or accepts
`--spec <file> --results <directory>`. The public
`simit::ci_runtime::group::execute` function uses the same typed contract. A JSON
spec has schema `simit.nix-group-spec.v1`, with `members`, `plan`, `check_systems`,
`limits`, `post_build`, `post_build_always` and optional `fresh_installables`.
Unknown fields, invalid membership and unsupported Nix flags fail before Nix
execution. The results directory must already exist and contain no earlier
group receipt or member evidence.

Retained `simit.nix-group.v1` receipts preserve source/tree/run/attempt/event,
ordered results, hook statuses and numbered member directories. Optional
`fresh_execution` is present only for fresh members. A fresh member must first
materialize successfully with valid output JSON, then pass current-worker
`--rebuild` with an explicit empty `builders` override, preventing configured
remote builders from replacing current-worker execution. Ordinary materialization
is never fresh acceptance. Fresh evidence
retains the transport predecessor's filenames: `build.log` for materialization,
`materialization-result.json`, `fresh-build.log` for rebuilding, and `result.json`
for the final result. Malformed successful output and failed builds/hooks fail the group while subsequent
members still run. Dispatch and process-limit failures are recorded as status
125; Unix signal termination retains the v1 negative signal status (for example,
`-9` for SIGKILL). Member stdout/stderr and hook output are retained as separate
files, and failed admission observations include their actionable stderr in the
CLI diagnostic.
Subprocess output is capped before evidence writes to 16 MiB stdout and 64 MiB stderr per command,
with a six-hour maximum process lifetime; configured workflow timeouts still
apply. Unix cancellation stops execution and terminates the current process
group rather than executing later members.
Accepted hooks up to 1 MiB execute from retained `.script` files, avoiding
platform per-argument limits. The generated workflow writes a private JSON spec
using a shell builtin instead of putting hooks into environment strings, and its
diagnostic fallback uses the same private-file transport. A small Bash wrapper
preserves `bash -c` argument identity, stdin and trailing script newlines.
The complete compact JSON spec must fit within 16 MiB, including JSON escapes.
Generation and library admission enforce the same budget as the CLI reader;
oversized combinations reject before project writes or runtime effects even
when every individual hook fits its 1 MiB limit.
Generated grouped workflows also have GitHub's 500,000-byte file limit. This
counts all embedded specs, repeated diagnostic fallbacks, YAML escaping and
transport steps; generation rejects overflow before writing project files.
The CLI requires a nonempty `--results` or `SIMIT_NIX_BUILD_RESULTS` evidence
directory and rejects missing or empty inputs before execution.
Without `--spec`, the runtime reads fresh members from the retained
`SIMIT_NIX_FRESH` JSON array. `SIMIT_NIX_FRESH_INSTALLABLES` is also accepted;
if both keys are set, their decoded lists must agree. Invalid or conflicting
values reject before dispatch or evidence writes.
The evidence root must have no prior receipt, inventory, coverage manifest or
numbered member entries. Interrupted and fallback-only attempts, including
out-of-range member indices, reject before Git/Nix dispatch or evidence writes;
choose a fresh evidence root rather than mixing attempts.
Output-reader startup failures return through the
same dispatch-failure path and clean up any started readers and child processes.
Embedding applications use `execute_with` with a caller-owned `Cancellation`
token and `Runner`. The library installs no process-global signal handlers. The
CLI owns one cancellation flag across its entire command lifetime, including
the gaps between subprocesses, and checks cancellation before every dispatch.

The shell-only diagnostic fallback remains cancellation-aware and runs after
setup, provisioning or admission failure. Its completion markers prevent
duplicate collection. The native integration suite executes the generated
invocation and this fallback using the actual packaged CLI at controlled Nix
process boundaries. These checks replace the authored Python group harness;
other Python fixtures retain their own packaging inputs until migrated.

Execution receipts are local evidence, not forge authority. Historical Python
v1 receipts remain readable as evidence, but a new Rust source needs its own
original-attempt hosted qualification. Offline integrity checks do not establish
current provider acceptance, merge readiness or publication authorization.

### Native dependency stream admission

`simit::ci_runtime::dependencies` ports the reviewed export-stream admission
boundary from signed Simit source `a9874535107dd6cf335ab7c4bdfd9a9252c0c691`.
Its `ArchiveAdmission` inputs must come from separately validated source/run
provenance and fresh dependency/qualification evaluation. They are byte and
inventory expectations, not qualification authority. The transport workflow's
provenance/evaluation/export policy adapters remain a separate migration slice.

`admit_archive` checks archive size and checksum while copying the compressed
bytes into a private descriptor. It decompresses only that checksum-bound
snapshot into another anonymous descriptor, then parses the **entire** strict
Nix writer grammar before returning a one-use `VerifiedArchive`. Both descriptors
are explicitly mode `0600` and unlinked on Unix. Replacing or modifying the
original archive after admission cannot replace the imported bytes.

The actual record set must exactly equal the admitted closure, include every
evaluated dependency root, and exclude all qualification outputs. Record paths
and deriver metadata use canonical `/nix/store` syntax; references must be
sorted, unique and wholly inside the closure. Legacy signature framing must be
zero. The terminal marker must be followed immediately by EOF, with no remaining
declared bytes. Parsing bounds include 100,000 paths, 1,000,000 nodes and
references, bounded strings and byte budgets, and streamed 64 KiB content reads.

Importer compatibility follows Nix **2.34.8** `src/libutil/archive.cc`: node
depth is strictly below **64**, directory names are at most **255 bytes**,
and symlink targets are at most **4095 bytes**. The first invalid value is denied
even in a second record after a valid first record, before any import effect.
Directory names are sorted as raw bytes, including non-UTF-8 names.
ASCII case aliases within a directory are conservatively denied on all platforms
before import, preventing Darwin's case-hack rewrites from colliding with real entries.

`VerifiedArchive::restore` dispatches one `nix-store --import` with the fully
rewound validated descriptor, then verifies admitted paths and observes evaluated
roots. Nonzero import/verification status produces no successful restore receipt.
All restore command batches are prepared before import against a 96 KiB combined
argv/environment budget, including string terminators and pointer tables. Path
batches additionally use at most 60 KiB. Commands inherit the same frozen,
accounted environment; an oversized environment fails before store mutation.
The envelope reserves at least 32 KiB beneath supported Linux's 128 KiB exec
floor and 160 KiB beneath Darwin's 256 KiB limit for platform/interpreter overhead.
The compressed envelope matches the transport producer's default zlib bound
(`maximum + (maximum >> 12) + (maximum >> 14) + (maximum >> 25) + 1 MiB`),
using checked arithmetic. These library checks do not complete the transport or
custody adapters' source/provider admission and zero-Nix-before-byte-admission gates.
`consume` supports a caller-owned importer with the same descriptor and one-use
lifetime. Restoration receipts always state `qualification_execution: false`;
fresh checks still require their separate current-worker rebuild.

Protocol sources:

- [Nix export/import framing](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/adbf23e8184bbbe8d786aad1f362443b6542e0a4/src/libstore/export-import.cc)
- [Nix 2.34.8 importer grammar and limits](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/2.34.8/src/libutil/archive.cc)

### Primary-only regeneration

Use the persisted project policy to regenerate verification and native-build
workflows during a dependency migration:

```sh
simit init ci --primary-only --check --diff
simit init ci --primary-only
simit init ci --primary-only --check --diff
```

This scope includes ordinary member/aggregate CI (including independent lanes), native Nix matrices and
prebuild workflows. Publisher, release, Pages and review workflows are preserved
byte-for-byte, together with `simit.toml`, release trust roots and README badges.
The check reports drift only in the selected scope. Full generation remains the
default; run its separate drift gate when intentionally changing publication
configuration. `--primary-only` cannot be combined with the other scope selectors.

Project templates are a separate owner, regardless of their output basename:
`ci-release.yaml` and `build-release.yaml` do not become primary CI. Scoped
generation validates declared template paths and destination protections but
does not load or render template sources, publisher or review material. Template
outputs retain their ownership markers after a mapping is removed; only full
generation retires them. Primary cleanup still removes obsolete marked built-in
CI workflows and preserves hand-owned files. Policy files such as `deny.toml`
are not created in this scope. Printed repair commands retain `--primary-only`
and the effective platform/provider, including Crow format overrides.

### Project-owned workflow templates

Projects with specialized Actions jobs can render their existing workflow
templates through Simit alongside its built-in jobs:

```toml
[ci.workflow_templates]
".github/workflows/tests.yml" = ".simit/templates/tests.yml"

[ci.workflow_variables]
runner = "${{ github.event.repository.fork && 'ubuntu-24.04' || 'ubuntu-latest-32-core' }}"
```

The template uses `@simit(runner)@` where this literal value belongs. Simit
substitutes named values once, preserving GitHub `${{ ... }}` expressions and
shell syntax. There are no recursive substitutions or implicit environment
reads. Undefined variables and malformed rendered YAML fail before any output
is written. Keep credentials as runtime Actions secret references, never literal
values in committed templates or configuration.

`simit init ci` renders the declared templates, marks their outputs as generated,
and persists both mappings and variables. `--check --diff` and registry auditing
use the same renderer, so edits to outputs, templates, or variables are detected.
Removing a mapping retires outputs carrying both Simit generation and template
markers, even when project comments precede those markers; unrelated workflows
remain project-owned. Built-in and release-owned workflow collisions, paths
outside the repository, and mismatched Actions platforms are rejected. Template
contents do not participate in built-in check, package, or runner inference.
Built-in generated workflows cannot be template sources: templates must remain
project-owned inputs, rather than snapshots of outputs from an earlier run.
Keep template sources outside Actions workflow directories, or give them a
non-workflow extension such as `.yaml.in`, so the source is not itself executed.
File identity is checked against both Actions workflow directories, so a hard
link with a project-template spelling cannot duplicate an existing active job.
Every source and destination component must be portable across supported hosts:
Windows device names, reserved characters, and trailing dots or spaces are rejected
before filesystem resolution. Destinations must be files with directory parents;
validation rejects existing directories, symlinks, portable case-insensitive path
collisions, and hard-linked aliases of template sources or planned outputs before
any writes. A destination also cannot alias a differently spelled active project
workflow through portable case/normalization or a hard link; declaring the exact
existing path retains explicit adoption behavior. Portable keys
use Unicode canonical normalization and full case folding, so non-ASCII and
composed/decomposed spellings cannot claim the same output. Existing aliases are
also checked against the actual filesystem, excluding symlink endpoints from
case/normalization alias matching. Generated files replace their own
directory entries atomically; an unrelated file hard-linked to a destination
retains its original bytes and file identity. Existing permissions are preserved.
This feature supports GitHub and Forgejo Actions, including exact-only Nix
qualification; it does not replace the
project's test selections or permission policy.

When importing upstream CI, retain its presets in template sources and declare
fork-specific policy through variables. Apply future upstream changes to those
sources, then regenerate rather than modifying generated workflow files.

### Provider-review merge gate

`canix-toolbelt` owns provider review, durable request accounting, and guarded
merging. Simit can generate its trusted `review-policy` coordinator separately
from ordinary CI and from the build-oriented `[review]` controller:

```toml
[ci]
platform = "github"
provider = "actions"

[review_policy]
toolbelt_version = "0.2.0" # select a qualified, published stable release
app_id_secret = "REVIEW_POLICY_APP_ID"
app_private_key_secret = "REVIEW_POLICY_APP_PRIVATE_KEY"
credential_environment = "review-policy"
# Optional policy from the trusted default-branch checkout, JSON or Pkl:
# policy_path = "policy/review.json"
```

Generate and verify with `simit init ci --platform github` and
`simit init ci --platform github --check --diff`. Do not enable a version before
its crates.io publication has been independently verified.

Provision a **dedicated policy GitHub App**, install it on each enrolled
repository. Store its ID/private key **only as secrets of the configured
credential environment**, and restrict that environment's deployment branch
policy to the repository's exact default branch. Do not also create
repository-level copies: a branch-controlled workflow could use those without
the environment boundary. The workflow's ref condition is an additional guard;
the platform-enforced environment restriction protects the credential when a
manual dispatch selects an edited non-default-branch workflow. Configure and
verify that boundary before enabling the coordinator.
This is separate from Greptile's installed App: Greptile supplies review records;
the policy App authenticates the normalized acceptance check. The policy App
needs repository `Checks: write`, `Contents: read`, `Pull requests: read`,
`Issues: read`, and GitHub's mandatory `Metadata: read`. Do not grant contents
write, administration write, or a merge credential to the coordinator.

The workflow executes only on the default-branch ref, checks out its exact
trusted event SHA with credentials disabled, and installs the exact locked
registry engine. It never executes PR source. PR/comment events reconcile
individual candidates; a bounded, ten-minute scheduled sweep covers completed
bot reviews, dismissals, and delayed feedback. Collection waits up to ten
minutes for event-triggered runs without requesting another provider review.
Scheduled sweeps enumerate every open-PR page, up to the supported 5000-PR
bound, collect without waiting in batches of twenty, and allow an active sweep
to finish before the next. Exceeding the bound fails explicitly without claiming
partial qualification. All findings remain
blocking until source fixes receive a fresh review or repository writers record
exact-finding evidence-backed dispositions.

After the first check is published, configure classic branch protection with
strict up-to-date checks and administrator enforcement. Require `review-policy`
with its **dedicated App ID**, plus the repository's actual required CI contexts
and human-approval policy. Do not bind the review context to the shared GitHub
Actions App: PR-controlled workflows can otherwise impersonate that context.
Unconfigured protection, absent credentials, unsupported rulesets/merge queues,
and missing or failed CI remain merge blockers.

The normal operator flow is `canix-toolbelt review ensure --pr URL`, investigate
and fix every confirmed finding, repeat ensure after each head change, then
`canix-toolbelt merge --pr URL --apply` for an authorized merge. Canix's direct
library consumer exposes the equivalent `canix repo review` / `canix repo merge`
surface once its qualified release is installed. A `ready` receipt cannot
replace the merge command's live revalidation.

### Rust feature coverage and MSRV environments

Rust Actions workflows honor `ci.all_features` for tests and Clippy in both
Cargo and Nix runtimes, including split-runner jobs and crates.io publishers.
Packages with features also get a separate `--no-default-features` pass. This
matters for libraries whose optional CLI is absent from their default features.

With `ci.with_msrv = true`, Cargo jobs install and select the declared
`package.rust-version`. Nix jobs select `devShells.<system>.msrv` and verify that
`rustc --version` matches that version before compiling all targets with the
configured feature policy. A default-shell alias pointing at a newer compiler
does not satisfy the MSRV gate.

Nix-runtime format checks use the declared `formatter.<system>` executable,
selected from `meta.mainProgram`, `pname`, or the derivation name. A treefmt
formatter runs with `--ci`; custom formatters run without assumed arguments,
then the gate rejects tracked, index, or untracked-file changes. A custom
formatter's nonzero exit status is preserved. A missing executable fails the
gate. Only projects without a flake formatter fall back to shell-provided
treefmt, then Cargo formatting when treefmt is absent.

New Rust flakes generated by `simit init flake` include the native `msrv` shell
when Cargo declares a minimum version. Full canonical generation also manages
`rust-toolchain-msrv.toml`, containing that normalized compiler version and the
minimal profile. The shell reads this source asset rather than `builtins.toFile`,
which does not materialize its result during read-only no-build evaluation.
Commit the manifest alongside the generated flake; parity checks reject a missing
or stale version. Hooks-only and custom modes preserve project-owned manifests.
Full canonical regeneration also migrates the recognized prior generated inline
MSRV binding before accepting hook wiring. Full checks report that migration as
drift. Modified or dynamic inline manifests require an explicit project edit;
Simit does not discard extra toolchain settings to force the migration.
Existing/custom flakes must provide the
same shell contract; hooks-only generation leaves their shells project-owned.
The generated `nix/rust-toolchain-msrv.toml` is source-owned and must be committed
alongside the flake, so read-only evaluation works in a fresh checkout.
Use Harbor's `lib.rust.mkToolchain` with an exact-version toolchain manifest and its
`mkCross`/`mkDevShells` helpers. Clear inherited nightly-only `RUSTFLAGS` and
`CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS` in stable/MSRV shells, and carry project-specific native
build dependencies into the MSRV environment.

Generated native Rust, cross Rust and Python flakes consume one exact-qualified
`github.com/caniko/harbor` input. Rust APIs live under `harbor.lib.rust`, Python
APIs under `harbor.lib.python`, and shared toolchain follows use `harbor/<input>`.
Existing project-owned flakes using standalone Harbor inputs keep their current
wiring during hooks-only generation; migrate their input, follows and API calls
together before retiring a standalone source.

### Publishing mode

Rust CI and crates.io publishing are separate modes. By default, `simit init ci`
generates ordinary CI workflows even when a package has crates.io metadata. It
does not generate `publish-crate*.yaml` or `keys/maintainers.gpg` unless release
publishing is enabled explicitly or inferred from existing generated release
workflows.

Enable crates.io release workflows with:

```sh
simit init ci --platform forgejo --publish-crates
```

Persist the choice when a project owns release publishing:

```toml
[ci]
publish_crates = true
```

Pass `--publish-crates=false` or set `publish_crates = false` to keep a project
CI-only even when stale generated publish workflows are present. Release
artifact and package-manager publishing flags such as `--with-artifacts`,
`--with-homebrew`, `--with-chocolatey`, and `--with-scoop` imply release mode.

Nix-only generation, including `[ci.nix_build].only = true`, rejects enabled
language/release options from either the command line or `[ci]`. This includes
`with_nextest`, `with_msrv`, `with_audit`, `with_deny`, `with_docs`,
`with_artifacts`, and `with_pypi_publish`. Put required checks inside the
declared Nix installables or use language CI. `publish_crates` is supported: a
Nix-only Cargo workspace receives the same per-member `publish-crate-*.yaml`
tag workflows and `trusted-publish-crate-*.yaml` publishers as aggregate
language CI, without language CI workflows. Under `only = true` the tag
workflow omits `nix flake check`, matching the primary CI. Members that depend
on each other require `publish_strategy = "coordinated"`, which emits the
dependency-ordered `publish-workspace.yaml` on GitHub instead. Explicit `--flag=false`
overrides disable the matching project option and persist that choice when
generating. Rejected requests leave configuration and workflow files intact.

For a Forgejo Nix workspace with release artifacts and cargo-deny:

```sh
simit init ci --platform forgejo --runtime nix --runner atlas-nix-trusted \
  --workspace --with-artifacts --with-deny --check --diff
```

Per-member GitHub and Forgejo workflows use package-qualified job names, such as
`my-crate / test` and `my-crate / gate-integration`. These are distinct required
check names even when several members use the same job IDs. Regenerate existing
workflows and select the qualified names in branch protection when adopting this
generator; single-package and aggregate workflow check names retain their shape.

If the project also publishes a Homebrew tap, keep the tap metadata in project
config when possible. Command-line overrides work, but config makes future
checks shorter and reproducible.

## Flake-Integrated Rust Projects

`--runtime auto` selects the Nix runtime when `flake.nix` exposes meaningful
project outputs such as `packages`, `apps`, `checks`, `devShells`, NixOS or
Home Manager modules, or top-level `lib`. Cargo-only projects and placeholder
flakes stay on direct Cargo CI.

For existing custom flakes, keep project-owned outputs intact and let simit
manage hook wiring with:

```sh
simit init flake --scope hooks-only
simit init ci --platform forgejo --runtime nix
```

## Focused Hosted Nix Builds

### Project-owned formatting

`simit init flake --scope full` wires the project treefmt policy into:

- `formatter.<system>` for `nix fmt`;
- `checks.<system>.formatting` for the uncached formatting gate;
- the development shell's packages for direct `treefmt` use;
- the pre-commit hook, using the same wrapper with `--ci`.

Rust and cross-platform shells use the pinned Rust formatter supplied to
`nix/treefmt.nix`; Python shells use the same treefmt wrapper for their own
language policy. Run `treefmt` inside `nix develop`, or use `nix fmt`.

Custom flakes retain ownership of their shell definitions. Include
`treefmtEval.config.build.wrapper` in `packages` (or Python `extraPackages`)
beside `pre-commit-check.enabledPackages`. `simit init flake --check --diff`
reports missing shell wiring; a comment or the formatter output alone does
not satisfy that check.

Generated Nix CI executes the project formatter with `--ci` and propagates
evaluation, build and formatting failures. A project with `nix/treefmt.nix`,
`treefmt.toml` or `.treefmt.toml` must provide the flake formatter output;
an ambient treefmt or a Rust-only check cannot substitute for its policy.
Legacy Nix projects without a treefmt policy retain their Cargo fmt gate.

Declare the exact installables that qualify a feature in `[ci].nix_builds`.
GitHub Actions projects can configure their matrix independently of ordinary
checks and release jobs:

For native multi-architecture builds, set `[ci.nix_build.system_runners]`:

```toml
[ci.nix_build.system_runners]
"x86_64-linux" = "ubuntu-24.04"
"aarch64-linux" = "ubuntu-24.04-arm"
```

Every installable must explicitly select a system, for example
`.#checks.aarch64-linux.cargo-test`, `.#packages.x86_64-linux.server`, or
`.#formatter.aarch64-linux`, and
that system must have a runner entry. The generator emits one job per declared
installable, rather than running each gate on every architecture. It verifies
the runner's OS/CPU identity independently of Nix configuration, then checks the
configured Nix system before project setup or realization. Linux, Darwin and
FreeBSD kernel names are recognized; unsupported kernels fail closed. With `kvm = true`,
KVM setup runs only for `x86_64-linux` rows; ARM rows do not require `/dev/kvm`.
The existing `[ci].runner` remains the runner for ordinary language CI. Without
the exact-build map, the installable matrix retains its single-runner behavior.
Standard `formatter.<system>`, `defaultPackage.<system>` and `devShell.<system>`
outputs select their system without a trailing name.
Output selectors such as `^out`, `^out,dev` and `^*` remain intact in generated
installables; routing extracts the system from the attribute path alone.
Node action versions follow
the mapped workers: if any mapped worker needs the compatible Node 20 baseline,
all rows use that baseline independently of the ordinary language CI runner.
Unambiguous PowerPC uname spellings (`ppc`, `ppcle`, `ppc64`, `ppc64le`) normalize
to Nix's corresponding `powerpc` names before comparison.

The map also supports `[ci.nix_build.groups]`: every group must contain only
installables for one system, and the group runs on that system's mapped runner.
Mixed-system groups reject before configuration or workflow writes. Group jobs
use the same hardware/Nix guard and x86 Linux-only KVM condition as ungrouped
rows, while retaining per-member evidence and hooks. Native mappings currently
cannot combine with `dependency_installables`: the single dependency producer
does not support native per-system routing, so this combination rejects before
writes rather than realizing foreign dependencies on one worker.

```toml
[ci]
platform = "github"
provider = "actions"
runtime = "nix"
runner = "ubuntu-24.04"
nix_builds = [
  ".#checks.x86_64-linux.client-runtime",
  ".#checks.x86_64-linux.managed-postgres-recovery",
]

[ci.nix_build]
only = true
timeout_minutes = 90
max_parallel = 1
max_jobs = 1
cores = 2
kvm = true
capture_results = true
artifact_retention_days = 14
extra_setup = ["python3 ci/prepare-input-access.py"]
post_build = ["python3 ci/retain-receipts.py"]
post_build_always = ["python3 ci/retain-diagnostics.py"]
artifact_paths = ["${{ runner.temp }}/receipts/**"]
required_secrets = ["FLAKE_SSH_KEY"]

[ci.nix_build.extra_env]
FLAKE_SSH_KEY = "${{ secrets.FLAKE_SSH_KEY }}"
```

Generate and check with `simit init ci --platform github --runtime nix`, then
`simit init ci --check --diff`. `only = true` supports flake-only, Rust and Python flake projects: it
emits `nix-builds.yaml` without a broad flake-check workflow. Switching to it
removes obsolete Simit-managed primary CI while preserving project-owned
workflows. It cannot be combined with `components`, `nix_system_runners`, or
language-specific release flags other than `publish_crates`; it coexists with `[prebuild]`,
which then publishes its own `[prebuild].nix_builds` subset. Without `only`, and only on a
GitHub Actions primary, the matrix coexists with `[prebuild]` once
`[prebuild].nix_builds` selects the published subset or `[ci.nix_build]` sets an
option; otherwise the prebuild realizes every `[ci].nix_builds` entry itself. Rust workspaces resolve this
policy from the workspace root, including invocations from member directories.
Select all required Rust checks explicitly as Nix installables in this mode.
Rust and Python projects can also use the other matrix options alongside their
ordinary CI.

The installable matrix qualifies branch pushes, pull requests, and explicit
dispatches. Its push trigger defines only `branches`, which excludes tag pushes
without a tag filter under GitHub's workflow rules. Channel-specific release
workflows retain their own triggers and publication policy.

The nested environment and setup apply only to the build matrix. Bind every
required secret to the same-named variable using `${{ secrets.NAME }}` under
`extra_env`; the generated preflight fails on a missing secret without printing
its value. GitHub supplies no repository secrets to fork pull requests, so these
credential-dependent jobs fail preflight rather than claiming qualification.
`required_env` checks run after setup, allowing setup to create credential files.
Keep private-input credentials out of global `[ci].extra_env` and release jobs.

KVM setup requires a GitHub-hosted Linux runner with `/dev/kvm`. Configured
matrix builds use `--no-update-lock-file`; `max_jobs` and `cores` bound Nix
realization, and `max_parallel` bounds the number of matrix jobs. Limits are
validated: timeout 1–360 minutes, parallelism 1–256, jobs 1–1024, cores 0–1024
(0 means all available cores), and artifact retention 1–90 days.

With `capture_results = true`, `$SIMIT_NIX_BUILD_RESULTS` points to a job-specific
runner-temporary directory containing the checked-out `revision`, selected
`installable`, `build.log`, and Nix's `result.json` (derivation and output paths).
The build preserves Nix's failure status while streaming and retaining its
diagnostics. `post_build` commands run after successful realization; they can
read `result.json` and copy package receipts or VM reports into the evidence
directory. They must fail if an expected receipt is missing. The pinned upload
action runs even after failure and includes any explicit `artifact_paths`.
Artifacts retain evidence, not Nix store closures; an empty or partial result
file after failure is not a passing receipt.

Use `post_build_always` for diagnostic collection that must run after a failed
build or setup step. These commands run with `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` before
artifact upload, honoring workflow cancellation. They must handle an absent or
partial build log and result map. A collector failure still fails the job, and a
successful collector never clears
the earlier build failure. Both post-build command lists require
`capture_results = true`. Keep qualification receipt validation in `post_build`.

Omitting `[ci.nix_build]` preserves the existing generated matrix defaults.

### Shared-store Nix groups

Rust projects using GitHub Actions with the Nix runtime can opt into
`[ci].independent_lanes = true`. The `rust` lane retains the existing format,
test, quality, docs, generator and package steps. The `evaluation` lane evaluates
the complete flake on all systems without building. Required-gate jobs qualify
the same immutable PR head as these lanes. Every lane adds Cargo's configured
binary directory before project setup. With the default `nix_flake_check = true`,
the `realization` lane also builds all flake checks. These lanes start independently
and retain the same push and PR triggers. Step-runner overrides and `om_ci` are
not supported together with this opt-in.

Setting `nix_flake_check = false` omits only the realization lane. Establish
complete discovered-check and declared-production-output coverage through the
groups below, qualify their receipts, then migrate required branch contexts
before removing overlapping full-flake realization.

Native required contexts change from `test` to `rust`, `evaluation` and,
when enabled, `realization` (with workspace member prefixes where applicable).
Enroll every applicable lane and group context before retiring `test`.

`[ci.nix_build.groups]` partitions every entry in `ci.nix_builds` into named
jobs. Related packages and checks share a fresh hosted runner's Nix store, so
their common dependencies are built once within that job. Group membership
must be complete, nonempty and disjoint; `capture_results = true` is required.
Grouped jobs provision an independently pinned native Rust engine. The separate
dependency-transport adapter provisions Python 3.12 through a pinned setup action
for its producer and consumer steps, including on custom runners.
An omitted `timeout_minutes` retains the runner's default job
timeout rather than introducing a group-specific limit.

```toml
[ci.nix_build]
capture_results = true
max_parallel = 4
max_jobs = 1
cores = 2
check_systems = ["x86_64-linux"]

[ci.nix_build.groups]
pinentry = [".#pinentry", ".#checks.x86_64-linux.pinentry"]
network = [".#checks.x86_64-linux.network"]
```

The example assumes those are all declared installables and all checks on the
selected system. `check_systems` discovers the actual check derivations before
realization and refuses an unassigned check. Include checks supplied by imported
flake modules too. Every group retains a source-bound coverage manifest and a
separate result, exit status and builder log for every installable. A failed
member fails the job while the other members still produce diagnostic evidence.
Post-build hooks run for each successful member with `INSTALLABLE` and
`SIMIT_NIX_BUILD_RESULTS` bound to that member's numbered evidence directory.
Grouped hook bodies cannot contain Actions expressions (`${{ ... }}`): GitHub
would expand them into retained spec and script files. Bind expressions through
`extra_env` and reference shell variables in hooks instead. Generated transport
variables in the `SIMIT_DEPENDENCY_*` namespace cannot be overridden by `extra_env`.
Diagnostic hooks run for every member, including after failed setup or admission;
a command-shell fallback collects any member skipped before the native build
loop. Completed diagnostic phases are marked to prevent duplicate collection.
Hook failures fail the group while remaining members still run. The transport
adapter's admission checks remain enforced when Python optimization is enabled.

Grouped jobs have `build (<group>)` contexts. Qualify the new evidence and migrate
required contexts together before retiring a monolithic flake-check gate.

Simit's `Qualify native grouped execution` workflow exercises the production
engine on fresh `aarch64-linux` and `aarch64-darwin` hosted workers. Each job
checks actual hardware before provisioning, builds the exact event-head engine,
and executes its generated native guard, immutable bootstrap, group invocation
and diagnostic fallback. The fixture qualifies both cold materialization and
warm-store rebuilds, requiring current-worker builder markers, ordered v1 member
receipts, successful hooks and no duplicate fallback collection. Artifacts retain
the source hashes, production derivation, engine digest, generated workflow and
per-state evidence. Only successful original-attempt jobs and independently
verified artifacts establish platform acceptance for that exact source; this
workflow does not enroll a consumer's engine variable or required contexts.

### Completion-driven producer custody

`[ci.custody]` generates a trusted default-branch `workflow_run` observer. Enroll
workflow names, source paths, every required job name and every required artifact
name. Branch/PR producers must use original attempt 1; the observer never reruns
producers and never checks out or executes their source or artifacts.

```toml
[ci.custody]
repository = "owner/repository"
producer_attempt = 1
status_context = "simit/producer-custody"

[ci.custody.producers.CI]
workflow = ".github/workflows/ci.yaml"
jobs = ["rust", "evaluation"]

[ci.custody.producers."Nix installable builds"]
workflow = ".github/workflows/nix-builds.yaml"
jobs = ["build (network)", "build (pinentry)"]
artifacts = ["nix-build-0", "nix-build-1"]
```

Existing policies retain the `strict-v1` protocol by default. Set
`protocol = "sealed-v2"` in `[ci.custody]` to select the prospective
[sealed-original custody contract](../ci-sealed-custody.md): capture each
completion immediately, seal complete evidence as an immutable artifact, and
independently verify exact capsules before aggregation and source-head reporting.
The following describes the default observer; v2's jobs, completeness admission
and installation-specific capsule lifecycle are documented separately.

GitHub executes `workflow_run` from the default branch and fires it when **any**
listed workflow completes. Install the observer on that branch before testing
it with candidate producers. The first event may record a pending observation;
the last completion aggregates every enrolled producer for the same source head,
branch and event. Duplicate identities, nonoriginal attempts, missing jobs or
artifacts, failed/skipped required jobs and incomplete custody cannot succeed.
GitHub filters completions by display name, which is not unique. A positively
identified workflow file outside every enrolled path is ignored before creating
a reporting target or collection queue, even if it reuses an enrolled name.
Capture and report repeat this early fence and never read stale receipts for
unrelated completions. An enrolled path with a wrong name or ref qualifier still
fails admission and revokes its established target.
Admission and bounded-capture checks use explicit errors and remain enforced
when Python optimization is enabled. Failed revalidation revokes a previously
successful observation in both ordinary and optimized interpreter modes.

The observer binds each producer's workflow definition through GitHub's native
[`WorkflowRun.file` / `WorkflowRunFile`](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/actions#workflowrunfile)
record, documented as an executed workflow file. Its repository, path, parent run,
attempt, event and check-suite repository must match the admitted original. The
`repositoryFileUrl` must identify an immutable 40-hex commit; custody fetches and
hashes the enrolled file at that revision, retaining the native response, commit,
Git blob metadata and workflow bytes. Each producer row records `workflow_revision`,
`workflow_tree` and `source_workflow_sha256`. The receipt's `head` / `tree` remain
the source-head identity, which can differ from the workflow-definition revision.

Raw REST `head_sha`, checkout logs, referenced reusable workflows and the current
PR merge ref are not substitutes for historical executed-file proof. This matters
when the base introduced or changed a workflow absent or different at the PR head.
Unavailable file records or mutable file URLs fail closed at the established
status target. Capture-final and post-upload report requery the native executed-file
record; revision drift revokes success in the same stable context. A native file
record at the raw head is admitted as that explicit provider proof, not inferred
from the source head. Installed-token access to these GraphQL records remains a
live acceptance gate.

The observer retains original jobs, provider log archives and required artifact
bytes. Archives are hashed without extraction. Capture and
API downloads share a 512 MiB wire budget; retained files and total archive
expansion each have a separate 512 MiB aggregate budget. At most 256 requests,
256 retained files and 10,000 archive members are admitted within a six-minute
capture deadline. Downloads and member hashes stream in 64 KiB chunks; oversized
or stalled provider downloads terminate and reap their own child processes.
Before constructing the ZIP reader, custody scans actual central-directory
records under a 16 MiB directory bound, the remaining aggregate member/expansion
budgets and the original deadline. Forged footer counts cannot bypass that scan.
Stored and deflated provider archives, including ZIP64, are supported; other
compression methods fail admission before any member decompression.
Enrollment accepts at most 100 jobs/artifacts across all producers. Generation
also admits the complete rendered workflow only up to 500,000 UTF-8 bytes under
GitHub's [500 KB workflow-file limit](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/actions/reference/limits#workflow-file-size),
including repeated policy/program text and YAML/JSON escaping. Oversized policies
reject before generated-file reconciliation or configuration persistence; shorten
enrolled names/inventories to fit. Capture budget failures retain the established
failure-reporting target.

Capture and upload must both complete before source-head status success. Reporting is
idempotent and explicitly targets the producer commit, not the observer's default-
branch SHA. Status contexts are `<status_context>/<event>/<target-sha256>`, using
the full SHA-256 of the canonical stable target identity: repository IDs and
normalized names, event, exact case-sensitive head branch, and, for PRs, PR ID,
number, base repository ID and exact base ref. The prefix is at most 22 UTF-8
bytes under Simit's 100-byte composed-context contract. Different PRs or bases
at the same commit cannot satisfy each other's contexts. Enroll the exact target
contexts before replacing existing protection. Repository names are compared
case-insensitively, matching GitHub's owner/repository naming rules.

PR custody requires exactly one valid provider PR association, including matching
head SHA/ref and repository IDs. Missing, ambiguous or malformed associations fail
without inventing a branch-only reporting target. Discovery, selected details,
capture-final and report-time revalidation bind the stable identity and observed
head/base SHA snapshots. Snapshot equality is conservative admission of observed
API data, not authenticated historical base-execution provenance. The observed
base SHA stays out of the status key so later changes can revoke the same target.

A token-free, contents-read identity job derives the full target digest before
collection. Collection uses that digest plus head SHA in job-level concurrency;
different branches, PRs, base refs and case-distinct refs have distinct queues.
Pending replacement within one target observes the same enrolled producer set.
The collect job reserves 25 minutes for six-minute capture, upload bounded to five
minutes, six-minute report lookups and a separate 90-second status POST. Reporting
runs after failed upload and exhausted lookup budgets to publish failure when the
completion target was safely established.

Same-repository branch/PR custody is supported; signed-tag release
attempt policy and fork custody require separately qualified enrollment.

The collect job has only contents/actions/checks read and statuses write
permissions. `checks: read` admits the native check-suite proof in private
repositories; identity remains contents-read and receives no token environment. It
provides observation custody, not independent execution acceptance. Keep native
test/build contexts and consumer receipt validation authoritative. Qualify its
default-branch installation, completion ordering, source-head reporting and
all-producer aggregation before replacing an existing waiting collector.
Use the [installed-observer acceptance procedure](../ci-custody-acceptance.md)
to retain both completion orders, isolation and live failure/revocation evidence.

Simit's own enrollment observes its native `CI/test` producer and a short,
source-bound `Custody qualification fixture` producer. The fixture uploads inert
Python text as archive data; the observer hashes it without executing it. Their
different completion times exercise pending-to-complete aggregation. Before the
observer is merged onto the default branch, candidate workflow runs qualify the
generator and fixture only. Retain the merged-source observer events and subsequent
branch/PR events to qualify installation, source-head reporting and ordering.

### CI dependency reuse

`[ci.cache]` declares public credential-free HTTPS substituters and signing keys
for CI independently of release publication. An explicit empty table disables
inherited release-cache settings; omitting the table preserves that inheritance.
Forgejo Actions applies the selected cache settings to its preinstalled Nix
environment, retaining existing `NIX_CONFIG`. Release publication continues to
use its separate release-cache policy.
Keep using `with_nix_cargo_cache = true` for the existing native Cargo cache.

```toml
[ci.cache]
substituters = ["https://cache.example.org"]
trusted_public_keys = ["cache.example.org:PUBLIC_KEY_BASE64"]

[ci.nix_build]
dependency_installables = [".#ci-patched-zellij"]
dependency_max_mib = 2048
fresh_installables = [".#checks.x86_64-linux.pinentry-runtime"]
```

Dependency transport requires groups and discovered `check_systems`. It builds
only selected build inputs in a separate fresh worker and exports their complete
closure to a same-run artifact. Enroll unselected local derivation attributes such
as `.#ci-patched-zellij`; transport builds every output. Explicit `^out`, `^dev`
and `^*` selectors are rejected before generation, both in dependency enrollment
and in qualification plans using dependency transport. Selectors in workflows
without dependency transport retain their existing behavior.
Transport-enabled qualification plans also require bare `.#attribute` local
derivations; remote and path references cannot drift between producer, import
admission and the group build. Both the dependency producer and consuming groups
inherit the runner's default timeout when `timeout_minutes` is omitted.

The compressed-size budget includes zlib's default worst-case DEFLATE expansion
plus gzip framing allowance. Export checks the same bound before marking an
archive complete that import checks before store effects; the uncompressed
budget is enforced separately throughout both streams.
Import admits compressed size, checksum and the complete decompressed byte
budget before derivation evaluation, which can itself instantiate store objects
or trigger IFD. The admitted bytes stay in one private, unlinked spool through
source/graph checks and import. Compressed bytes are privately snapshotted too:
checksum and decompression read the same snapshot, even if the downloaded inode
changes afterward.

Consumers verify source commit/tree, lock bytes,
repository, run, attempt, expected derivations/output paths, archive checksum and
transport budget before importing. The consumer parses the full Nix export/NAR
stream without extraction: actual records must exactly match the admitted closure
and every declared reference stays inside it. Duplicate, missing, extra, malformed,
truncated or trailing records reject before any canonical-store import. Parsing
bounds paths, references, tree depth/nodes and control fields, and streams file
payloads in 64 KiB chunks. NAR depth is less than 64; entry names and symlink
targets are at most 255 and 4095 bytes, respectively, matching the
[Nix 2.34.8 importer limits](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/2.34.8/src/libutil/archive.cc).
These bounds apply to the entire stream before import, including later records.
Admission conservatively rejects ASCII case aliases within each directory on
all platforms. Darwin's default case hack can otherwise rewrite an alias into
an existing `~nix~case~hack~` entry and fail partway through import. Nearby suffix
names without aliases and names in separate directories remain supported.
Validation and import use the same unlinked, mode-0600
spool descriptor. The parser follows [Nix's export framing](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/adbf23e8184bbbe8d786aad1f362443b6542e0a4/src/libstore/export-import.cc)
and [NAR writer grammar](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/adbf23e8184bbbe8d786aad1f362443b6542e0a4/doc/manual/src/protocols/nix-archive.md).
Legacy export signatures are rejected; archive integrity is distinct from hosted
producer authority. An alias of a discovered check or a declared
qualification output is refused. A failed dependency producer blocks consuming
groups; its builder and export diagnostics remain available.

Artifacts are bound to the exact run **and attempt**. Use **Re-run all jobs**
after a consumer failure so the dependency producer also executes in the new
attempt. GitHub's **Re-run failed jobs** can retain a successful producer from
the previous attempt; its artifact is intentionally not accepted by retried
consumers. There is no fallback to prior-attempt or cross-run artifacts.

`kvm = true` enables hosted KVM on both the dependency producer and each consuming
worker before custom setup or builds. Export and post-import verification also
admit their complete argument vectors against the current worker's `ARG_MAX`,
charging inherited environment strings and pointer arrays with platform headroom.
A byte-budget-valid closure can still exceed this process limit; it is rejected
before export, or before any import when verification would exceed the consumer's
limit. Independently terminated export streams are never concatenated.

`fresh_installables` first materializes cold outputs and dependencies normally,
then requires an explicit `--rebuild` on the current worker. Nix check mode needs
valid outputs, so an uncached check can execute twice; materialization alone never
constitutes acceptance. Both direct aliases and transitive qualification outputs
are rejected from dependency transport before export/import. Keep
VMs and other runtime checks in this explicit fresh set, and measure export,
download/import and cache-hit costs alongside end-to-end latency.

`cache_installables` reuses heavy local build inputs across runs, such as a
patched kernel that only a VM gate consumes. It requires groups and accepts bare
`.#attribute` derivations that are neither qualification outputs, `checks`, nor
transported dependencies:

```toml
[ci.nix_build]
cache_installables = [".#nixosTests.x86_64-linux.vm.nodes.machine.boot.kernelPackages.kernel"]
```

Each grouped job resolves every entry to its exact derivation and restores the
GitHub Actions cache key `simit-nix-input-v1-<derivation hash>` without restore
keys, so a changed input is a miss and builds normally. A hit imports all of the
derivation's outputs and their closure before the group runs, unless that
closure contains an output of one of the group's qualification members; that
fails the job instead of silently skipping a gate. An unreadable entry is
ignored. After the group runs, including when a member failed, entries the job
realized but did not restore are exported and saved, up to 4 GiB each. Cache
scopes are GitHub's: pull requests read default-branch entries and write only
their own scope. Imports skip signature checks, so declare only inputs whose
producers you trust as much as the default branch.

Configured matrices normally coalesce a branch push with its pull request. Set
`[ci.nix_build].separate_events = true` when acceptance requires both original
producers: the concurrency group then includes the workflow ref and event name,
so a PR cannot cancel its corresponding push. Newer revisions still supersede
older runs within each event stream. Retain cancelled predecessors as failures;
their receipts cannot substitute for either required successful producer.

Aggregate Rust CI also coalesces push and PR events by default. Set
`[ci].separate_events = true` when both Rust CI originals are required. This
GitHub Actions opt-in retains workflow, event, source-repository and ref identity
in the concurrency group, so fork PRs remain isolated and newer runs can
supersede older runs within each event stream. It is independent of
`[ci.nix_build].separate_events`; configure both when acceptance requires both
originals from ordinary Rust CI and the Nix matrix. Nix-only and Python CI reject
the Rust setting instead of silently ignoring it.

Nix matrices qualify branch pushes by default. Set
`[ci.nix_build].push_tags = ["**"]` to also qualify every tag push, including when
adopting a workflow that previously used an unfiltered `push:` trigger. More
selective GitHub tag patterns and ordered exclusions are supported, for example
`push_tags = ["v*", "!v*-preview"]`. A nonempty list must include at least one
positive pattern. Tag patterns survive regeneration and drift checks; omitting
them retains the branch-only default. Tag-enabled coalescing keeps tags separate
from same-named branches and pull requests while coalescing a branch's push and PR.

## Required Integration Gates

Project-owned custom flakes declare additional required gates without
hand-editing generated YAML:

```toml
[[ci.required_gates]]
id = "gel-integration"
run = "nix run .#test-gel"
timeout_minutes = 30

[[ci.required_gates]]
id = "gel-check"
run = "nix flake check --no-write-lock-file"
timeout_minutes = 30
env = { GEL_FIXTURE = "local" }
```

Each gate has a stable `id`, one explicit single-line `run` command (a `nix
run`, `nix build`, or `nix flake check` invocation for flake targets), a
bounded `timeout_minutes` (1–360, default 30), and scoped `env`. Gates render
as dedicated `gate-<id>` jobs in CI (same push/PR triggers, once per run) and
as credential-free prerequisite steps in the coordinated publisher at the exact signed
revision. Any gate failure blocks publication. Gate setup lives in `run`/`env`
only — never in global `[ci].extra_setup`, so publishing and artifact jobs do
not inherit test-only services or credentials. Release secrets
(`CRATES_IO_API_TOKEN`, minisign, etc.) must never appear in gate `env`; they
belong only to independent default-branch upload jobs in the protected
`simit-crates-io` environment.

On GitHub Actions, a gate can retain diagnostic files after success or failure:

```toml
[ci.required_gates.artifacts]
name = "gel-evidence"
paths = ["target/evidence/", "e2e/test-results/"]
retention_days = 14
```

Place this table immediately after the gate it belongs to. Artifact names must
be valid and unique across gates. Names and paths cannot have surrounding
whitespace: the upload action trims inputs rather than preserving those names.
Retention defaults to seven days and accepts 1–90 days. Uploads use `always()`
with the gate step's outcome: failed gates retain evidence, but skipped or
not-started gates cannot publish stale files under their names. Missing files
warn; the gate's failure still blocks publication. Uploads are bounded to five
minutes and use the action version compatible with the effective runner.
Hidden files within explicitly selected paths are included; exclude sensitive
files explicitly, even when they start with a dot.

Artifact-bearing CI gates apply `timeout_minutes` to the command step and give
the job fifteen extra minutes for setup and upload, so their configured command
timeout must be at most 345 minutes. Other gates retain their existing limit.
Signed-source and trusted verification jobs reserve ten setup minutes plus all
gate command deadlines and five minutes per diagnostic upload, with a minimum
job limit of sixty minutes; larger existing job limits are retained.
Configurations exceeding the shared 360-minute
publishing job limit are rejected, including hosted-release validation jobs;
independent CI gates do not share that limit.
Workflow/job cancellation can still prevent an upload; this is diagnostic
retention, not an external custody guarantee.

Relative paths follow the gate's source checkout, including the isolated
signed-source checkout in trusted crate verification. Absolute, tilde and leading
expression paths (for example `${{ runner.temp }}/evidence`) remain unchanged.
For isolated trusted verification, leading expressions must directly reference
`runner.temp` or `github.workspace`, whose values are absolute. Other leading
expressions are rejected because their rootedness is unknown. Put variable
subdirectories after a literal relative prefix (for example
`target/${{ vars.EVIDENCE_SUBDIR }}/report.xml`) or use a literal path instead.
Artifact expressions cannot reference the `env` context: upload actions do not
inherit candidate gate environments. Use literal values or `runner`, `github`
or `vars` contexts instead.
Artifact names and paths in credential-free publishing cannot reference GitHub
secrets or authentication contexts. Signed-tag source builds
also retain gate failures before the success-gated trusted publisher can start.
Their diagnostics use `<artifact-name>.source` to avoid crate archive names.
Trusted crate publishers use `<artifact-name>.<package-name>` to avoid collisions
between gate/member pairs, including hyphenated names. Hosted-release validation
uses `gate.<artifact-name>` to avoid the reusable prebuild's `release-<system>`
and `flake-inputs-<system>` artifact namespaces. Ordinary CI names are unchanged.
Forgejo and Crow reject
this GitHub-only option after CLI backend overrides are resolved; hosted release
generation checks its effective release backend independently of the CI default.

## Coordinated Workspace Publication

Member-scoped publishing (`publish-crate-<crate>.yaml`) has no cross-crate
ordering. For lockstep workspaces that need prerequisites before dependents,
opt in (GitHub Actions only in v1):

```toml
[ci]
workspace = true
workspace_strategy = "aggregate"
publish_crates = true
publish_strategy = "coordinated"
```

```sh
simit init ci --platform github --runtime nix --workspace --workspace-strategy aggregate --publish-crates --coordinated-publish
simit init ci --platform github --check --diff
```

Switching strategies removes only obsolete simit-owned outputs (generated
`publish-crate-*.yaml` and `trusted-publish-crate-*.yaml` vs generated
`publish-workspace.yaml` and `trusted-publish-workspace.yaml`); handwritten
workflows are never deleted. Other backends (Forgejo, Crow, GitLab) fail
explicitly instead of silently degrading.
